strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP problem: coordinating heterogeneous open-source LLMs without retraining a separate router for every model.

The proposed SMACS framework is modular and conceptually clear: retrieval-based prior selection identifies suitable referencers, while exploration–exploitation posterior enhancement constructs and ranks multiple aggregations.

The empirical scope is broad, spanning eight benchmarks across mathematics, reasoning, medical question answering, instruction following, and code generation, with 15 open-source models, five closed-source models, and six collaboration baselines.
The appendix provides useful implementation details, including dataset splits, model lists, inference configurations, hyperparameters, and prompts, and a code release is promised.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. SMACS is a many-call ensemble—seven selected referencers plus multiple aggregator calls and substantial offline precomputation—whereas the main closed-source comparisons are single API models. There is no latency-, cost-, or call-count-matched comparison, nor a comparison against a closed-source ensemble.

The reported upper bounds are misleading. The per-task closed-source upper bound uses the best model for each benchmark, so it is not one deployable system. In Table 1, SMACS beats that per-task maximum on only three tasks, ties on one, and loses on four; a higher macro-average does not justify the unqualified claim that it beats closed-source LLMs.

There are serious numerical inconsistencies. The eight SMACS scores in Table 1 sum to 607.37, giving an average of 75.92, while the table reports 76.92 and the text states 76.78. Consequently, the advertised gains over GPT-o3-mini, GPT-4.1, and Claude-3.7-Sonnet cannot be verified from the table. The Average entries for the upper-bound rows are likewise not macro-averages of the displayed per-task values.

The posterior scoring is under-specified and potentially unsound. In Equation 7, S_i^PPL = 1 - PPL(G_i) is not generally bounded in [0,1] unless perplexity is normalized, but no normalization is defined. The model and tokenizer used to compute perplexity are not specified, and adding it directly to a cosine-similarity score lacks calibration.

Mean pairwise similarity primarily measures consensus among aggregations and can reward generic or mode-collapsed responses rather than correctness. The paper does not show that this hybrid score reliably correlates with ground-truth answer quality.

Important reproducibility details are missing, especially the value of K_drop, the random seeds, the perplexity scorer, and the exact procedure for constructing repeated reference subsets. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run variance are reported for stochastic generation.

It is unclear whether the fixed aggregator and hyperparameters were selected using only validation data. If the aggregator-selection experiments in Appendix A.4 used the reported test benchmarks, that would constitute test-set model selection.

The common 8,192-token setting disadvantages deep-reasoning models such as QwQ-32B, which is reflected in their low Table 1 scores. Although the 32,768-token appendix partly addresses this, the headline result relies on the restrictive setting. Identical prompts and decoding parameters also do not guarantee fairness across model families.

RPS requires a labeled question bank and offline responses from every LLM in the pool. Most retrieved support questions come from the same benchmark, and there is no leave-one-task-out or truly unseen-domain evaluation, so the generalization and scalability claims remain weakly supported.

The scaling analysis does not specify the order in which LLMs are added and does not report random-order controls or variance. The ablation gains are small, and the prose appears to swap the standalone RPS and mean-pairwise-similarity improvements shown in Table 2.

The technical novelty is incremental: instance-level routing, capability profiles, mixture-of-agents aggregation, voting, self-consistency, and best-of-n selection are already established. The contribution is mainly their combination and empirical engineering.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important NLP problem: coordinating heterogeneous open-source LLMs without model retraining.

SMACS is conceptually clear and practically useful: RPS profiles black-box LLMs from a unified question bank, while EPE explores multiple aggregated responses and selects among them at inference time.

The experimental scope is broad, spanning eight benchmarks across mathematics, reasoning, medical question answering, instruction following, and code generation, with 15 open-source models from 20B to 72B parameters.
The paper compares against five closed-source models and six existing collaboration approaches, and reports scaling curves and component ablations rather than only final accuracy.
Appendices provide useful reproducibility information, including dataset splits, model details, hyperparameters, inference settings, and prompts.
The main results support the narrower claim that a diverse open-source ensemble can outperform individual flagship closed-source models on average.
weaknesses: The closed-source upper-bound analysis contains an apparent inconsistency: GPT-o3-mini is reported at 73.33% on AIME, while the upper-bound row appears to use a much lower value. Taking the actual per-dataset maxima gives a closed-source oracle average of roughly 76.2%, reducing SMACS's default-setting margin to under one percentage point, rather than the reported +2.04%. This must be corrected or explained.

No confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or multi-seed variance are reported. Several gains are small and some benchmarks, especially AIME, contain few questions, so robust superiority is not established.

The hybrid posterior score is under-specified. The paper does not state which model computes perplexity or how perplexity is normalized; since 1-PPL is not generally bounded like cosine similarity, adding the two terms with lambda=1 is difficult to interpret.

Mean pairwise similarity primarily measures consensus and may penalize a uniquely correct but minority answer. More direct evidence that the hybrid score selects correct candidates would strengthen the method.

Some evaluation choices need clarification: the fixed Llama-3.3-70B aggregator appears to have been selected on benchmark performance, and using LiveCodeBench v6 as validation for a v5 test set creates a temporal mismatch. Retrieval of near-similar validation questions also warrants contamination and random-retrieval controls.

The comparison is compute-asymmetric: 15 reference models and multiple aggregator calls are compared with single closed-source responses, while latency, monetary cost, and energy are not analyzed. The term scalable therefore refers mainly to adding models, not efficient deployment.

The title and abstract are broader than the evidence: SMACS does not beat the best closed-source model on every task, including GPQA, LiveCodeBench, and MedMCQA, and no closed-source ensemble baseline is included.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, combining retrieval-based routing, response aggregation, consensus scoring, and perplexity filtering rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant NLP problem: making multi-LLM collaboration scalable without training a new router for every model.

The two-stage design is coherent and practically motivated. RPS provides black-box, instance-level prior selection, while EPE explores multiple reference subsets and repeated aggregations before selecting a final response.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, spanning eight mathematical, reasoning, instruction-following, and code-generation benchmarks, with fifteen open-source LLMs, five closed-source models, and six collaboration baselines.

The paper reports useful cost, latency, scaling, out-of-distribution, and ablation analyses. The appendix supplies model lists, hyperparameters, inference settings, and task-specific prompts, supporting reproducibility.

The reported average gains over both closed-source models and existing collaboration methods are practically meaningful, and the component ablation indicates that RPS, prior-based dropping, similarity scoring, and perplexity scoring all contribute.
The limitations section is candid about computational expense and the use of uniform inference configurations.
weaknesses: The central comparisons are somewhat asymmetric. SMCS uses labeled in-domain validation questions, historical LLM performance on those questions, fifteen reference models, and multiple aggregations, whereas the single closed-source LLMs do not receive the same retrieved validation context. A stronger evaluation would include equal-data baselines such as retrieved few-shot or RAG-augmented closed models, and the claims of surpassing closed-source LLMs should be qualified accordingly.

Scalability is not cost-free: adding an LLM still requires evaluating it across the entire labeled question bank, an O(RN) preprocessing cost that is not quantified. The approach also assumes access to labeled validation data, which may be unavailable in genuinely new domains.

The hybrid posterior score is not fully justified theoretically. Mean pairwise similarity can reward consensus or generic groupthink rather than correctness, while the model used to compute perplexity is not explicitly identified. The use of 1 - PPL without normalization and a fixed lambda also warrants sensitivity analysis.

Statistical evidence is limited. Repetitions are conducted for only four datasets and three seeds, with no paired significance tests, confidence intervals for baseline comparisons, or baseline variance. Several task-level gains are small and may not be robust.
The scaling curves lack error bars and do not specify or average over model-addition order, so the apparent monotonic improvement may depend on which LLMs are added first.

The novelty is mainly integrative: nearest-neighbor routing, response dropout, repeated aggregation, self-consistency, and perplexity/embedding reranking are already established techniques. The paper does not introduce a substantial new algorithmic principle beyond their combination.

The claimed out-of-distribution generalization is mostly cross-dataset generalization within familiar math, code, and reasoning task families; the question bank still contains closely related task domains.

There are reproducibility and clarity gaps: the promised code URL is not visible in the reviewed version, some notation in Equation 6 is difficult to parse, the cost-price snapshot is unspecified, and the fixed aggregator appears to have been selected after benchmark-level experimentation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important NLP problem: coordinating heterogeneous black-box LLMs without task-specific router training.

The two-stage design is practical and model-agnostic. Retrieval-based prior selection keeps inference focused on a small top-K subset, while repeated subset aggregation provides a straightforward way to explore multiple combinations.

The empirical scope is broad, spanning eight benchmarks across mathematics, complex reasoning, instruction following, and code generation, with fifteen open-source LLMs and several multi-LLM baselines.

The paper includes a useful range of analyses: component ablations, scaling curves, OOD retrieval experiments, aggregator comparisons, longer-output experiments, cost/latency measurements, and repeated runs on several datasets.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including model lists, dataset splits, hyperparameters, benchmark prompts, and the aggregator prompt, which helps reproducibility.
The reported improvements over strong collaboration baselines such as MoA, Self-MoA, and Symbolic-MoE are promising, although they require further validation.
weaknesses: The posterior selection criterion is not sufficiently justified as a measure of response quality. Mean embedding similarity mainly captures consensus/style, while perplexity mainly captures fluency; neither directly verifies correctness. The paper does not specify which LM computes perplexity, whether it is conditioned on the question and references, or how robust the score is across models and domains.

The perplexity term $1-PPL(\cdot)$ is unbounded and not normalized, despite being added with $\lambda=1$ to a similarity score in $(0,1]$. The empirical observation that perplexity is usually between 1 and 2 does not replace a principled normalization or robustness analysis.

The model-selection protocol may involve test-set tuning. Figure 7 selects the aggregator using five of the main evaluation benchmarks, but the paper does not clearly state that these experiments used validation splits only. The choice of hyperparameters and benchmark-specific prompts also needs a validation-only protocol.

The headline comparisons to individual closed-source LLMs are not apples-to-apples. SMCS uses fifteen reference LLMs plus repeated aggregations, whereas GPT-4.1 and GPT-o3-mini are single models. The best-per-open-model row is also mislabeled as an 'upper bound'; an ensemble exceeding a single-model baseline is not surprising without equal-compute controls.

The novelty is primarily an engineering combination of existing ideas: nearest-neighbor routing, historical correctness matrices, subset aggregation, consensus scoring, and perplexity-based ranking. The exploration-exploitation framing remains heuristic and lacks a formal analysis or measured diversity guarantee.

Scalability is only partially established. Adding an LLM still requires evaluating it on the entire labeled question bank, and adding a task requires labeled support questions. Offline onboarding cost, memory usage, and retrieval cost as the bank grows are not measured.

Statistical rigor is limited for the main claims. There are no confidence intervals or significance tests against the principal baselines, repeated runs are reported for only four datasets, and the averaging rule behind the 'Avg' column is not clearly reconciled with the per-benchmark scores.

Several reproducibility details are missing or incomplete: the abstract promises code but no URL is shown, the exact perplexity implementation is unclear, API settings and seeds for closed models need clarification, cost assumptions and hardware are not fully specified, and the model ordering used in the scaling curves is not stated.

The paper would benefit from deeper failure analysis, including cases where prior retrieval selects the wrong experts, where the hybrid score chooses a fluent but incorrect aggregation, and how sensitive the method is to prompt changes or a weaker aggregator.
